items.risk: Risk: a rich language becomes the real product; the typed Spec becomes a veneer.
items.title: Package recipe surface: how much language is allowed?

items.risk: Risk: subtle non-reproducible builds and broken caches.
items.title: Cross compilation and multi-arch closures

items.risk: Risk: base becomes a special snowflake lane.
items.title: Kernel/userland split: pkgbase vs “derive base”

items.risk: Risk: the secure path is too hard; people bypass it.
items.title: Update distribution strategy

items.risk: Risk: beautiful theory, miserable incidents (if we never ship the human-scale views).
items.title: Human-scale debugging

items.risk: Risk: unclear target leads to conflicting security postures.
items.title: Desktop/interactive workload stance (if any)

items.risk: Risk: fleets silently fall out of rollback coverage.
items.title: Store growth + GC + long-lived fleets

items.risk: Risk: users reinvent unsafe sharing (mount whole home everywhere) or admins keep homes always mounted (data exposure at rest).
items.title: Human identity + home data model (portable homes vs host accounts)

items.risk: Risk: fuzzing becomes a vanity dashboard, while regressions still require heroics.
items.title: Continuous fuzzing + regression localization (signal vs noise)

items.risk: Risk: secure boot becomes a checkbox while attackers (or accidents) still control which kernel code runs.
items.title: Kernel module policy + loader verification (don’t leave a pre-kernel hole)

items.risk: Risk: a single untrusted USB device collapses the security posture, or users invent ad-hoc bypass workflows.
items.title: Removable media + device posture (USB is the universal footgun)

items.risk: Risk: the system reverts to mystery bytes, and the safe open path becomes optional folklore.
items.title: Origin labels + quarantine metadata (prevent laundering and stripping)

items.risk: Risk: either networking becomes ambient again, or users/admins train themselves to bypass the safe path.
items.title: Outbound network policy + consent UX (avoid silent exfil or click-ops)

items.risk: Risk: hard-coded witness lists (centralization) or brittle availability requirements.
items.title: Witness networks as security parameters (availability, diversity, governance)

items.risk: Risk: security checks degrade into “ignore expiry” during incidents, which becomes normal.
items.title: Trustworthy time in hostile environments (rollback-by-clock, offline bootstrap)

items.risk: Risk: services quietly become internet-facing, and incidents cannot answer *what was exposed and why*.
items.title: Inbound exposure + firewall state (avoid ambient listeners and port-folklore)

items.risk: Risk: models drift from implementation/intent and become diagramware; the lane becomes theatre instead of a safety tool.
items.title: Formal methods lane: models become stale or theatre

items.risk: Risk: approvals become “click until it works” or a purely social process that attackers bypass.
items.title: Quorum approvals: click-ops, bypass, and governance drift

items.risk: Risk: either the identity lane becomes an overbuilt “mesh”, or it stays absent and people reintroduce static secrets.
items.title: Workload identity + credential issuance (avoid "static token" relapse)

items.risk: Risk: enforcement is perceived as brittle, so it's disabled or bypassed, and the system returns to ambient execution from writable areas.
items.title: Exec integrity enforcement: brittleness and bypass

items.risk: Risk: supply chain checks devolve into "it's signed, ship it" with weak identity semantics.
items.title: Keyless identity receipts: over-trust and identity confusion

items.risk: Risk: remote support becomes a permanent backdoor, or recording becomes surveillance; either outcome trains users to bypass the safe path.
items.title: Remote assistance + session recording: backdoors, stealth, and privacy drift

items.risk: Risk: frontend tooling becomes a large, fast-moving TCB that operators bypass or that silently changes semantics.
items.title: Spec/policy authoring frontends: compiler trust and DSL sprawl

items.risk: Risk: either metadata is too hard to use (people ignore it), or it becomes ambient surveillance/exfiltration.
items.title: Queryable metadata: privacy, laundering, and index integrity

items.risk: Risk: the ecosystem invents unofficial composition patterns that bypass provenance, policy, and explainability.
items.title: Multi-origin userlands: explicit strata vs ad-hoc chroots

items.risk: Risk: runtime policy becomes folklore; review/diff tooling loses leverage.
items.title: “How it runs” source vs runtime artifact sprawl (component descriptors)

items.risk: Risk: components become overprivileged; sandbox primitives exist but are not used in practice.
items.title: Permission creep despite explicit grants (need authority budgets)

items.risk: Risk: the optimization becomes an unreviewed distribution path, or it becomes an ambient surveillance surface.
items.title: Lazy mounts and partial fetch: integrity, side-channels, and fallback drift

items.risk: Risk: snapshots become a silent data-exfil path and undermine least-authority promises.
items.title: Snapshot UX vs security: revocation, secret retention, and ambient exposure

items.risk: Risk: operators deploy P2P daemons outside the Derive trust/evidence model, or P2P becomes a stealthy exfil surface.
items.title: P2P distribution: poisoning, identity confusion, and privacy leakage

items.risk: Risk: operability features become a new exfiltration surface or a compliance nightmare.
items.title: Structured diagnostics vs privacy (Inspect trees can become ambient surveillance)

items.risk: Risk: performance regressions, covert channels, or an ecosystem split where the real debugging happens outside the Derive evidence model.
items.title: Flight recorders: overhead, covert channels, and “debug mode” bypasses

items.risk: Risk: trust roots drift silently, TLS validation becomes inconsistent across libraries, and incidents can't answer "what roots were trusted".
items.title: Trust bundles: format choice, interop renderers, and drift control

items.risk: Risk: either hostname policy devolves into folklore again, or DNS evidence becomes too sensitive to keep/ship.
items.title: DNS mediation receipts: TOCTOU control vs privacy toxicity

items.risk: Risk: operators fall back to file-based keys and ad-hoc agents, or the broker becomes an unreviewable, omnipotent signing daemon.
items.title: Crypto operations portal: key abuse, user presence, and audit toxicity

items.risk: Risk: expiry-based security becomes a bypass (“clock was wrong”), or operators add ad-hoc time tooling outside the Derive evidence model.
items.title: Trustworthy time: quorum failures, expiry safety, and operational response

items.risk: Risk: installation is too brittle or scary, operators bypass the Derive model, and recovery devolves into unreceipted folklore tooling.
items.title: Installation and recovery: disk layout idempotency, encryption ergonomics, and “don't wipe the wrong disk”

items.risk: Risk: either operators keep static keys and bypass the Derive model, or we build an access broker that is too complex, too central, or too privacy-toxic to adopt.
items.title: Operator access leases: JIT cert UX, audit value, and "no backdoor" posture

items.risk: Risk: the lane exists “on paper” but is too painful to adopt, so secrets/update gates drift into bespoke vendor tooling outside the Derive evidence model.
items.title: Measured boot in practice: event-log replay ergonomics, attester lifecycle, and variance policy

items.risk: Risk: fleets accumulate “feel-good backups” that cannot be restored, or build shadow backup tooling outside the Derive evidence model.
items.title: Backups and restore drills: key availability, privacy, and false confidence

items.risk: Risk: kernel state becomes mutable folklore, undermining verification claims and making incident response depend on guesswork.
items.title: Kernel mutation control: sysctls, boot tunables, and module loading drift

items.risk: Risk: we either under-specify the lane and upgrades keep bricking hosts, or we over-collect identifiers and the evidence model becomes privacy-toxic.
items.title: Hardware inventory + compatibility gates: safety, privacy, and operability

items.risk: Risk: firmware and boot policy drift happen outside the Derive evidence model, undermining attestation, trust-bootstrap claims, and upgrade safety.
items.title: Firmware updates + UEFI variable drift: trust roots, remote bricks, and unreceipted platform mutation

items.risk: Risk: networking becomes folklore again — remote incidents require SSH log spelunking, drift breaks reproducibility claims, and topology changes become a top-3 remote brick vector.
items.title: Network topology drift: routes, addresses, pf substrate, and remote-brick changes

items.risk: Risk: `/dev` becomes folklore again, sandboxing claims are undermined, and permission creep happens via invisible device exposure.
items.title: `/dev` drift: ambient device nodes, devfs ruleset folklore, and sandbox escapes

items.risk: Risk: A–D becomes an untestable promise and the archive drifts toward a single implicit product shape.
items.title: Product profiles (A–D) as first-class compilation targets

items.risk: Risk: deployments invent ad-hoc key handling that leaks secrets or makes recovery folklore.
items.title: Data-at-rest posture (ZFS encryption + keys + recovery)

items.risk: Risk: B becomes infeasible, forcing forks or abandoning the workstation story.
items.title: Desktop viability constraints (even if desktop is not v0)

items.risk: Risk: exports revert to folklore (“someone emailed a tarball”), making incidents less explainable and turning support tooling into an exfiltration footgun.
items.title: Export boundary drift: policy changes, redaction defaults, and exfil risk

items.risk: Risk: admission control becomes folklore (“we totally check attestation”), turning attestation into theater and enabling accidental (or malicious) permission expansion.
items.title: Attestation admission policy drift: keep “what is gated?” stable and reviewable
